analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to study and minimize the cost of new rules on small businesses before issuing them.
analysis.headline: Two House committees approved the bill in December 2013, but the House never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend a 1980 law that already requires federal agencies to analyze how new rules affect small businesses. It would make those analyses much more detailed, add new steps where the Small Business Administration's Office of Advocacy reviews major rules before they are proposed, allow agencies to waive nothing, and open the door to court challenges of rules for sloppy small-business analysis. It also requires agencies to keep periodic lists of rules affecting small businesses and consider amending or rescinding them.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that would face federal regulation, along with the trade associations that represent them. The bill gives them more chances to weigh in before rules are proposed, a formal review panel for major rules, and a new legal hook to challenge rules in federal appeals courts. Note that the bill's definition of a covered 'small organization' extends to nonprofits with up to $7 million in net worth and 500 employees, so the shield reaches well beyond mom-and-pop shops.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated businesses and their trade associations

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would have to estimate the cumulative effect of all federal rules on affected small businesses and describe alternatives that minimize those costs before issuing a rule.

For major rules, the Small Business Administration's Chief Counsel for Advocacy would convene a review panel and file an assessment of the rule's impact on small entities, including energy and start-up costs, before the rule is proposed.

The bill removes agencies' existing ability to waive or delay the initial small-business analysis and gives the SBA Chief Counsel power to issue binding compliance rules and intervene in agency proceedings.
Businesses could sue over a rule's failure to comply with the small-business analysis requirements, with review heard by federal courts of appeals.

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies would bear much heavier analysis and reporting duties, and the public would bear the cost of delayed or weaker rules: where a rule protects workers' wages and safety, consumers' finances, or the environment, months of added analysis, comment rounds, and litigation would slow or dilute the protection.

drawbacks.text: The added analysis, review panels, and court challenges are designed to slow rulemaking; for rules that protect wages, health, safety, or consumers, delay and dilution are the point, and the public bears that cost.

The 'small entity' definitions are generous to regulated firms, covering organizations with up to $7 million in net worth and 500 employees, so the procedural shield would extend to businesses far larger than the family shop the bill's name evokes.
Expanded judicial review handed to courts of appeals would give regulated parties a recurring procedural tool to relitigate rules on process grounds even when the substance is lawful.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some provisions are genuinely modest and useful on their face, such as clearer agency agendas, plain-language compliance guides, and input from women-, veteran-, and minority-owned firms on reviewing old rules. But the bill's core is procedural friction: every major rule would pick up extra analysis, a review panel, and a litigation hook. Whether that is a fair balance depends on whose rules are being delayed; for rules protecting workers, consumers, and the environment, the cost lands on the people the rules are meant to protect.

outcome.mechanism: Both House committees sent the bill to the House floor calendar in December 2013, but no one ever scheduled a floor vote, and the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 27, 2013 and referred to the House Judiciary and Small Business Committees.
The Judiciary Committee first ordered it reported by a recorded vote of 15-9, then, after amendment, ordered it reported again by voice vote in September 2013.
On December 11, 2013, both committees reported the bill with amendments, and it was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 208.
No further House action followed, the Senate never considered it, and the bill received no floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies are better off, since they never had to absorb the bill's added analysis, review-panel, and reporting duties. Regulated businesses lost the procedural shield the bill would have created, and rules protecting workers and consumers were not saddled with its delay-and-litigation mechanisms.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies; the bill's extra process never arrived

industries.industry: Regulated businesses and their trade associations
industries.note: The bill would give regulated firms more pre-proposal access to agencies, formal review panels for major rules, and a court hook to challenge rules over small-business analysis. Those gains come at the cost of slower and more contestable protections for workers, consumers, and the public.

Small firms would get more formal input, plain-language compliance guides, and periodic agency review of burdensome rules. Ordinary people are also small-business customers and employees, so the benefit is real but modest, and the broader procedural shield extends to much larger firms.
The pre-proposal review report would have to assess a rule's impact on the energy costs small entities pay, giving energy-cost arguments a formal place in the rulemaking record for every major rule.

Agencies would face detailed cumulative-impact analyses, mandatory notification and materials turnover to the SBA, review panels, annual review reports, and litigation over compliance, delaying the rules they are charged with issuing.
